units.title: Introduction and Graphics Hardware
topics: The frame buffer and its arithmetic
The graphics pipeline and the GPU
Seeing the ideas: pixels, tubes, tables and the pipeline

sections.title: The frame buffer and its arithmetic
The graphics pipeline and the GPU
Seeing the ideas: pixels, tubes, tables and the pipeline

summary: Graphics covers modelling, rendering, animation and image processing; applications range from CAD to games to maps.
Raster displays store every pixel and give filled colour images with aliasing; vector displays store lines and scale perfectly.
Frame-buffer size = width × height × bits ÷ 8: 1920 × 1080 × 24 bits needs 62,20,800 bytes and about 373.2 MB/s at 60 Hz.
A look-up table trades colour range for memory; double buffering prevents flicker.
The pipeline runs from modelling through viewing, projection, clipping and rasterisation to display, and GPUs execute it in parallel.

units.title: Scan Conversion - Lines, Circles, Ellipses and Area Filling
topics: Seeing the ideas: pixel grids, decisions and symmetry

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: pixel grids, decisions and symmetry

summary: Scan conversion picks pixels for primitives; step along the major axis and update an error term.
DDA: steps = max(|Δx|, |Δy|), increments Δ/steps, round at each step; Bresenham uses p₀ = 2Δy − Δx and integer updates 2Δy or 2(Δy − Δx).
Midpoint circle: p₀ = 1 − r, update by 2x + 1 (inside) or 2(x − y) + 1 (outside) with eight-way symmetry; midpoint ellipse uses two regions with four-way symmetry.
Scan-line fill uses the odd–even rule; boundary and flood fill spread from a seed; antialiasing uses supersampling or coverage.

units.title: Two-Dimensional Transformations and Viewing
topics: Coordinate systems and the window-to-viewport transformation
Seeing the ideas: moving shapes, order and the viewport

sections.title: Coordinate systems and the window-to-viewport transformation
Seeing the ideas: moving shapes, order and the viewport

summary: Homogeneous coordinates (x, y, 1) turn translation into matrix multiplication; sequences collapse into one matrix applied right to left.
Translation, scaling, rotation, reflection and shear have standard 3 × 3 matrices; rotation matrices are orthogonal with determinant 1.
Order matters: translate-then-rotate differs from rotate-then-translate.
Rotation or scaling about a point is T(p) · R or S · T(−p).
Window-to-viewport mapping scales and shifts with sx and sy; unequal factors distort.

units.title: Clipping
topics: Seeing the ideas: region codes, parameters and polygon clipping

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: region codes, parameters and polygon clipping

summary: Clipping discards geometry outside the window; efficient algorithms accept or reject trivially before computing intersections.
Cohen–Sutherland: a 4-bit outcode per endpoint; OR = 0 accepts, AND ≠ 0 rejects; otherwise cut at one boundary and repeat.
Liang–Barsky: pₖt ≤ qₖ; t₀ = max of entering r, t₁ = min of leaving r; at most two intersections.
Sutherland–Hodgman clips a polygon against each boundary in turn with four in/out cases; concave polygons need Weiler–Atherton.

units.title: Three-Dimensional Transformations, Projection and Viewing
topics: Seeing the ideas: axes, perspective, frustum and culling

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: axes, perspective, frustum and culling

summary: 3D transformations are 4 × 4 matrices; rotations about x, y, z are orthogonal matrices with determinant 1; order of composition matters.
Orthographic projection drops z; perspective projection divides by depth: x′ = x·d/z, y′ = y·d/z, via a matrix and a perspective divide.
Perspective causes foreshortening and vanishing points; parallel projection preserves parallel lines and sizes.
Viewing needs an eye, a look-at point and an up vector, a view volume (frustum) and a pipeline ending in the viewport transform.
Back-face culling tests N · V > 0 using the polygon normal.

units.title: Visible Surfaces, Illumination and Shading
topics: Seeing the ideas: depth buffers, vectors, highlights and shading

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: depth buffers, vectors, highlights and shading

summary: The Z-buffer keeps the nearest depth per pixel and works for any surface; painter's algorithm sorts and overwrites; back-face culling removes rear faces.
The Phong model is ambient + diffuse (N · L) + specular (R · V)ⁿ; Blinn–Phong uses N · H.
Flat shading uses one intensity per polygon, Gouraud interpolates vertex intensities, Phong interpolates normals and lights every pixel.
Gouraud shading can miss a highlight inside a polygon; Phong shading captures it.
Textures, shadow maps, alpha blending and ray tracing add realism.

units.title: Curves, Surfaces and Computer Animation
topics: Seeing the ideas: curves, continuity, easing and morphing

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: curves, continuity, easing and morphing

summary: Parametric curves with control points give designers local, predictable shape control; continuity is described as C⁰, C¹, C².

Bézier curves use Bernstein weights, pass through the end points, lie in the convex hull and are evaluated by de Casteljau subdivision; the cubic B-spline gives C² continuity and local control but does not pass through the end points.
3D shapes are polygon meshes, patches, subdivision surfaces, CSG or procedural models.
Animation uses keyframes and interpolation; easing (smoothstep 3t² − 2t³) replaces robotic constant speed; morphing interpolates corresponding vertices.
A 90-second 24 fps full-HD clip is 2,160 frames and 13.44 GB uncompressed.
